issues.legal_issue: Property comprising inseparable ancestral and non-ancestral portions is treated as non-ancestral unless the portions can be identified.
material_facts: The disputed lands included property descended from a common ancestor, a share acquired from another holder, and an estate later purchased by descendants.
The ancestral and non-ancestral portions of the lands could not be separated or identified.
issues.conclusion: The disputed lands were non-ancestral because their ancestral and non-ancestral portions could not be separated.
issues.legal_principle: Under Avtar Singh v. Thakar Singh, 35 I.A. 206, mixed lands whose ancestral and non-ancestral portions cannot be separated are regarded as non-ancestral unless the portions are shown. Inder Singh v. Gulzara Singh, A.I.R. 1951 Punj. 345, relying on Saif-ul-Rahman v. Mohammad Ali Khan, I.L.R. 9 Lah. 95, and Jagtar Singh v. Raghbir Singh, I.L.R. 13 Lah. 165, supports the principle that land ceases to be ancestral when it comes into an owner's hands otherwise than by descent.

predicates.inheritance_dispute: The dispute concerns the inheritance of property.
predicates.ancestral_and_non_ancestral_land_mixed: The land includes portions that came by descent and portions acquired otherwise than by descent.
predicates.ancestral_portions_cannot_be_identified: The ancestral portions of the mixed land cannot be separated or identified.

issues.definition: When an inheritance dispute concerns land containing mixed ancestral and non-ancestral portions that cannot be identified, the land is treated as non-ancestral.

issues.legal_issue: Where a custom excluding sisters and their sons from non-ancestral property is not established, succession to that property is governed by personal law, under which the sister takes in preference to the collateral.
material_facts: The deceased's sister and the son of another sister claimed the estate in preference to the deceased's fourth-degree collateral.
The relevant customary answer stated that sisters or their sons did not succeed, but it applied to ancestral property.
The courts found the property non-ancestral and found no evidence establishing a custom excluding sisters and their sons from non-ancestral property.
The courts below applied personal law in allowing the claim.
issues.conclusion: The courts below correctly applied personal law, and the sister and her sister's son were entitled to succeed in preference to the collateral.
issues.legal_principle: Customary answers of the kind recorded in the Riwaj-i-am apply to ancestral property; no custom excluding sisters from non-ancestral property was established here. Paragraph 24 of Rattigan's Digest, which states that sisters are excluded from inheritance to non-ancestral property, is too widely stated. The Court relied on Ujagar Singh v. Mst. Jeo, [1959] Supp. 2 S.C.R. 781, and Waryam Singh v. Smt. Sukhi, Civil Appeal No. 452 of 1961, decided April 23, 1963. In the absence of an applicable proved custom, personal law governed and preferred the sister to the collateral.

predicates.inheritance_dispute: The dispute concerns competing claims to inherit a deceased person's property.
predicates.property_is_non_ancestral: The property at issue is non-ancestral.
predicates.customary_exclusion_not_proved: No applicable custom excluding the sister from succession to the non-ancestral property is established.

issues.definition: In an inheritance dispute over non-ancestral property, if no applicable custom excluding the sister is established, the sister is preferred to the collateral under personal law.
